title: When Risk Becomes Personal: What Security Leaders Can Learn From a Cancer Diagnosis
content_md: Risk management leaders educate people on measuring exposure, testing assumptions and advising on how best to prepare for incidents they hope won’t occur. They know that the absence of a security alert does not stand for safety; that resilience depends on preparedness, and that a plan is only as good as the people who can execute it. But when the risk is personal, those ideas take on a heavier meaning. Receiving a Cancer Diagnosis I was diagnosed after a routine physical that included a PSA blood test. I had not noticed any symptoms and had no known family history. That raised a few eyebrows and ultimately, a stage-three prostate cancer diagnosis. My experience is not a case for making a personal health choice or offering clinical advice. That’s far from my wheelhouse. However, it is a helpful framework for a profession that often talks about preparedness, leadership and resilience, but sometimes forgets to consider the people expected to deliver all three. Risk Appetite Changes When the Asset is You In professional life, leaders can be admirably objective. They can challenge a security control, decide whether a certain risk falls within an agreed tolerance, and explain to a board why a difficult trade-off is necessary. They are typically analyzing a faceless enterprise. Risk management is more than recommending a set of analytical frameworks.
